query: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization but a low coercive field, and reported single-phase fcc high-entropy alloys derived from it have coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe in the reported magnetic measurements. What single intervention could overcome this coercivity limitation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted change relative to single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a matched derivative, the relevant compositional, structural, and measurement boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Introduction of a secondary phase with a high magnetocrystalline anisotropy constant via precipitation of a Co-rich phase can increase the coercive field of fcc FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its high-entropy alloy derivatives
generation.intervention: Thermal annealing to induce precipitation of a Co-rich phase
generation.conditions: Annealing temperature between 500°C to 700°C, annealing time between 1 hour to 10 hours
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitation of a Co-rich phase with high magnetocrystalline anisotropy constant
generation.mechanism: The introduction of a secondary phase with high magnetocrystalline anisotropy constant can act as pinning sites for domain walls, increasing the energy required for domain wall motion and thus increasing the coercive field
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in coercive field by at least a factor of 5 compared to the single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its high-entropy alloy derivatives
generation.baseline: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its high-entropy alloy derivatives with coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe
generation.boundary: Compositional boundary: FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys with a maximum of 10% deviation from the equiatomic composition; Structural boundary: fcc crystal structure with a secondary phase precipitated via thermal annealing; Measurement boundary: Magnetic measurements performed at room temperature
generation.uncertainty: The actual increase in coercive field may vary depending on the specific annealing conditions, composition, and microstructure of the alloy

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy samples with varying annealing conditions, measure the coercive field using a vibrating sample magnetometer or a physical property measurement system, and characterize the microstructure using transmission electron microscopy or X-ray diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coercive field of the annealed samples does not increase by at least a factor of 5 compared to the single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its high-entropy alloy derivatives, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The present work exhibits the effects of Sn addition on the magnetic properties and microstructure of FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The results show all the samples consist of a mixed structure of face-centered-cubic (FCC) phase and body-centered-cubic (BCC) phase. The addition of Sn promotes the formation of BCC phase, and it also affects the shape of Cu-rich nano-precipitates in BCC matrix. It also shows that the Curie temperatures (Tc) of the FCC phase and the saturation magnetization (Ms) of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs increase greatly while the remanence (Br) decreases after the addition of Sn into FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA. The thermomagnetic curves indicate that the phases of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs will transform from FCC with low Tc to BCC phase with high Tc at temperature of 600–700 K. This work provides a new idea for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs for their potential application as soft magnets to be used at high temperatures.

However, there is only little change for the value of magnetization as the temperature continues to increase. This is because only a small number of FCC phase transform to BCC phase according to the results of XRD in Figure 1 and DSC curves in Figure S1. Therefore, it can be concluded that the addition of a minor amount of Sn can obviously increase the Curie temperature of FCC phase. The phases of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs will transform from FCC with low Tc to BCC phase with high Tc at temperature of 600–700 K, which leads to the increase of magnetization. This provides a new idea for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs for their potential application as soft magnets to be used at high temperature.

In this work, the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs were prepared by vacuum arc-melt casting. Effects of Sn content on the phase constitution and magnetic properties were studied. All the samples are composed of FCC and BCC phases, whereas some unknown phases appear with the addition of Sn. The addition of Sn promotes the formation of BCC phase, and it also affects the shape of Cu-rich nanoprecipitates in the BCC matrix. Moreover, the Ms increases greatly while the remanence (Br) decreases with the increasing of x for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs. The addition of Sn can obviously increase the Curie temperature of the FCC phase. The phase of alloys with a mixture of FCC and BCC will transform from FCC to BCC phase at high temperature, leading to an increase of magnetization. They can be used as new soft magnetic materials at high temperatures.
